abstract: This paper presents a preliminary lexical and phonological reconstruction of Proto-Tangkhul (PTk), the ancestral mother language of the Tangkhulic branch within the Tibeto-Burman family. Based on extensive field data collected across Ukhrul (Standard Tangkhul), Huishu, Kachai, East Tusom, and Phadang, we establish regular sound correspondences between onset stops, liquid clusters (*pl-, *kl-, *pr-, *kr-), and vowel developments. We demonstrate that Standard Tangkhul underwent lenition of syllable codas while peripheral varieties like Huishu and Tusom preserved archaic conservative distinctions.

sections.title: 1. Introduction & Genetic Subgrouping
sections.content: The Tangkhulic languages, spoken primarily in Ukhrul and Kamjong districts of Manipur and adjoining regions of Myanmar, constitute an independent, deeply conservative branch of Tibeto-Burman. Grierson (1903) categorized them under the generic rubric 'Kuki-Chin-Naga', but subsequent historical work (Matisoff 1972, Burling 2003) confirmed their discrete genetic status. Standard Tangkhul (Ukhrul) functions as the literary standard and regional lingua franca, yet individual villages preserve distinct daughter languages with varying degrees of mutual intelligibility.

sections.title: 2. Phonological Correspondences & Syllable Structure
sections.content: Proto-Tangkhul possessed a sesquisyllabic or disyllabic structure *Cə-CVC. Modern Standard Tangkhul preserves the unstressed nominalizing/adjectival prefix *kə- (written ka-) and negative *mə- (written ma-). In Kachai, these prefixes undergo secondary voicing assimilation (gə- / bə-). In coda position, Proto-Tangkhul *-(k, t, p) are realized as unreleased glottal stops or weak stops in Ukhrul, whereas final *-l is lost in Ukhrul but preserved in Huishu.

sections.title: 3. Tonal Categories & Pitch Contours
sections.content: Proto-Tangkhul tones correlate systematically with syllable coda sonorancy and proto-voicing. Standard Ukhrul distinguishes three level tones: High (55), Mid (33), and Low (22). Stems ending in original voiceless stops condition High abrupt pitch, whereas sonorant codas allow tonal register contrasts that interact with morphological suffixation.

title: A Reconstruction of Proto-Tangkhulic Rhymes
alternate_titles: Diachronic Phonology and Coda Developments in Tangkhulic
subject: Historical Phonology & Sino-Tibetan Rhymes
notes: Landmark LTBA study demonstrating the regular diachronic evolution of rhymes from Proto-Tibeto-Burman to Proto-Tangkhulic.
abstract: We reconstruct the rhyme system of Proto-Tangkhulic (PTk) based on a comparative corpus of over 800 cognate sets spanning Standard Tangkhul (Ukhrul), Huishu, Kachai, Champhung, and Tusom. We demonstrate that Proto-Tangkhulic distinguished phonemic vowel length before dental and velar codas (*-a:t vs *-at; *-a:k vs *-ak), and retained the Proto-Tibeto-Burman lateral coda *-l, which merged into front glides or open vowels in Standard Tangkhul. This reconstruction resolves longstanding anomalies in the external comparison of Tangkhul with Jingpho and Lolo-Burmese.

sections.title: 1. The PTk Rhyme Inventory
sections.content: The reconstructed rhyme inventory of Proto-Tangkhulic includes 24 distinct rhymes with stop and nasal codas: *-am, *-an, *-aŋ, *-ap, *-at, *-ak, *-a:t, *-a:k, *-im, *-in, *-iŋ, *-ip, *-it, *-ik, *-um, *-un, *-uŋ, *-up, *-ut, *-uk, and lateral rhymes *-al, *-il, *-ul. While Standard Tangkhul regularly neutralizes vowel length before codas, the conservative Huishu dialect preserves qualitative differences that verify the length distinction.

sections.title: 2. Evolution of Lateral Codas (*-l)
sections.content: One of the major breakthroughs of Proto-Tangkhulic historical phonology is recognizing the regular fate of PTB *-l. In Standard Ukhrul, PTB *-l vocalized to a high front offglide [-i] after back vowels (e.g. *tul > tui 'speech'; *ŋul > ngui 'silver/money'). In Huishu, *-l is preserved intact as an alveolar lateral continuant [-l], proving that lateral loss in Ukhrul was a secondary innovation of the central dialect group.

sections.title: 3. Implications for Sino-Tibetan Subgrouping
sections.content: Recognizing the conservative nature of Proto-Tangkhulic rhymes provides a crucial benchmark for the genetic classification of the Indo-Burma borderlands. Tangkhulic shares specific rhyme mergers with Maring and Kuki-Chin, yet preserves distinct prefixal morphology that establishes it as a primary coordinate branch of Tibeto-Burman.

alternate_titles: Morphological and Etymological Parallels in Tangkhul and Sino-Tibetan
journal: Sino-Tibetan Etymological Dictionary and Thesaurus (STEDT) Monograph

abstract: This foundational paper analyzes the historical phonology and lexical morphology of Tangkhul Naga in the context of Proto-Tibeto-Burman (PTB) reconstruction. We examine over 120 basic vocabulary items from Pettigrew (1918) and Bhat (1969), identifying regular sound laws linking Tangkhul velar prefixes (kə-), nasal prefixes (mə-), and sibilant causatives (sə-) to pan-Sino-Tibetan morphosyntactic patterns. Tangkhul provides indispensable evidence for the antiquity of Tibeto-Burman sesquisyllabicity and nominalizing prefixation.

While spoken in relative geographical proximity to the Meithei (Manipuri) kingdom and the Kuki-Chin hills, its grammatical structure preserves ancient prefixal paradigms that have eroded in more isolating languages of Southeast Asia. Rev. William Pettigrew's 1918 grammar and dictionary provided early linguists with their first systematic view of this archaic system.

sections.title: 2. Prefixal Morphology and Derivational Functions
sections.content: In Tangkhul, verbal roots rarely occur bare in citation form. Instead, they carry the ubiquitous prefix ka-, which functions simultaneously as an infinitive marker, action nominalizer, and adjectivalizer (e.g., pha 'be good' -> kaphā 'good'). Negative clauses replace this with the discontinuous morpheme ma-...-mana. Causatives are derived through suffixal -sak or archaic stem-initial aspiration, directly parallel to the Tibetan s- causative prefix.

title: Tangkhul-Naga Grammar: A Study of Word Formation and Morphology
alternate_titles: Morphological Processes and Derivational Grammar of Standard Tangkhul
publisher: Department of Linguistics, Manipur University, Canchipur
subject: Descriptive Linguistics & Morphology
notes: Comprehensive descriptive grammar of Tangkhul word formation by native scholar Dr. Victor Ahum.
abstract: This study provides the first comprehensive modern morphological analysis of Standard Tangkhul Naga by a native linguist. Focusing on word-formation strategies, the dissertation examines the typology of roots, derivational prefixes, inflections, and compound formations. We investigate nominal compounding (endocentric and exocentric), reduplication, verbal valency alterations, and postpositional case affixation, demonstrating how Tangkhul balances agglutinating morphology with analytic syntax.

sections.title: 1. Morphological Typology & Root Classes
sections.content: Tangkhul word formation operates primarily through agglutination with strict suffixal dominance in nominal inflection and prefixal dominance in verbal derivation. Monosyllabic lexical roots fall into three major syntactic categories: Noun roots (shim 'house', ram 'country'), Verb roots (sa 'do', thei 'see', zat 'go'), and Deictic/Particle bases (hi 'this', chi 'that'). Nominal roots can occur bare as free morphemes, whereas verbal roots generally require affixes or compounding.

title: Aspiration Dissimilation and Phonological Rules in Tangkhul Naga
alternate_titles: Experimental Laboratory Phonology of Tangkhul Stop Consonants
journal: Carnegie Mellon University Working Papers in Linguistics
publisher: Department of Philosophy & Linguistics, Carnegie Mellon University
subject: Phonetics & Laboratory Phonology
notes: Experimental acoustic phonetic investigation of Grassmann's-law-like aspiration dissimilation in Tangkhul prefixal paradigms.
abstract: In Tangkhul Naga, prefixal stop consonants exhibit systematic aspiration dissimilation reminiscent of Grassmann's Law in Indo-European. When a verbal root begins with an aspirated stop (pʰ-, tʰ-, kʰ-), the preceding nominalizing/infinitive prefix surfaces as an unaspirated stop [kə-]. Conversely, when the verbal root begins with an unaspirated stop or sonorant, the prefix is realized with robust aspiration [kʰə-] in conservative varieties. Using acoustic measurements of Voice Onset Time (VOT) and burst spectra from 8 native speakers, this paper confirms that aspiration is a syntagmatically governed feature bounded by the phonological word.

sections.title: 1. The Phenomenon of Aspiration Dissimilation
sections.content: Phonologists have long studied long-distance consonant interactions such as consonant harmony and dissimilation. In Tangkhul, the interaction between the prefix consonant and the root-initial consonant exhibits a classic Obligatory Contour Principle (OCP) effect for the feature [spread glottis]. Two adjacent syllables within the same phonological stem cannot both surface with contrastive aspiration.

sections.title: 2. Acoustic Methodology & Voice Onset Time (VOT)
sections.content: Acoustic recordings of 120 prefix-root words were analyzed in Praat. Burst duration, Voice Onset Time (VOT), and vowel fundamental frequency (F0) perturbation were quantified. Aspirated root onsets showed mean VOTs of 68-85 ms, while unaspirated root onsets averaged 12-22 ms. The prefix vowel duration showed compensatory shortening when preceding aspirated roots, indicating a prosodic foot-level timing constraint.

sections.title: 3. Theoretical Phonological Implications
sections.content: These findings demonstrate that Tangkhul prefixal alternation is not mere morphological suppletion, but an active phonological rule governed by laryngeal licensing. It provides one of the few well-documented non-Indo-European cases of Grassmann's Law in the Sino-Tibetan language family.

title: Towards Morphological Processing and Computational Analysis of the Tangkhul Language
alternate_titles: Natural Language Processing and Morpheme Segmentation for Tangkhul NLP
journal: Computational Linguistics & Natural Language Processing Journal
publisher: Centre for Endangered Languages & NLP Research Forum, Manipur
subject: Computational Linguistics & NLP
notes: Groundbreaking computational paper outlining tokenization, morpheme segmentation, and grammatical particle frequency in Tangkhul corpora.
abstract: Building language technology for indigenous, low-resource languages requires robust morphological analyzers and clean corpora. In this paper, we develop a computational pipeline for the Tangkhul language spoken in Manipur, India. Using a digitalized corpus of 150,000 words extracted from curriculum textbooks and folklore anthologies, we analyze token frequency distributions, morpheme boundaries, and syntactic function words. We implement a rule-enhanced finite-state segmenter that handles complex affixation, achieving an F1-score of 88.4% on out-of-vocabulary root identification and lemmatization.

sections.title: 1. Linguistic Background & Digital Resource Gap
sections.content: Despite possessing over 180,000 speakers and a century of published literature in Roman script, Tangkhul remains severely under-represented in modern computational language resources. Standard tools like spaCy and NLTK fail on Tangkhul text due to agglutinative suffix chains and unique function particles. We address this resource gap by compiling a standardized tokenized corpus and establishing baseline segmentation benchmarks.

sections.title: 2. Affix Segmentation Architecture
sections.content: Tangkhul verbs inflect through sequential agglutination: [Prefix] + Root + [Aspect/Valency] + [Tense/Mood] + [Clause Linker]. For example, the surface word 'i-thei-ser-ra-kaji' decomposes into root thei 'see', completive -ser, future -ra, and quotative -kaji. Our finite-state transducer segments these affix clusters systematically, resolving morphophonemic boundary adjustments.

sections.title: 3. Evaluation & NLP Applications
sections.content: We evaluated our morphological analyzer on a gold-standard annotated test set of 2,500 sentences. The system achieved 91.2% precision and 85.8% recall on boundary detection. We demonstrate applications in bilingual dictionary search, computer-assisted language learning (CALL), and keyword extraction for digital heritage repositories.

subject: Descriptive Linguistics & Expressive Morphology
notes: Classic paper on expressive morphology, acoustic iconicity, and echo word formation in Tangkhul by CIIL linguist Dr. S. Arokianathan.
abstract: In South Asian and Tibeto-Burman languages, reduplication and echo word formation constitute vital expressive devices imparting vivid sensory imagery and grammatical plurality. This paper investigates the phonological rules and semantic categories of reduplication in Tangkhul Naga. We distinguish between complete lexical reduplication (e.g., zingsho-zingsho 'daily'), partial reduplication with vowel alternation (e.g., chir-char 'bustling commotion'), and rhyming echo compounds that denote generalized collectives ('X and associated items').

sections.title: 1. Morphological Types of Reduplication
sections.content: Tangkhul reduplication operates at both inflectional and expressive levels. Type I consists of complete lexical repetition where a nominal or temporal base is duplicated to signify distribution or intensity. Type II consists of partial reduplication where the onset consonant is copied while the nucleus vowel or coda undergoes apophonic alternation (often high vowel to low vowel).

sections.title: 2. Echo Words and Generalized Collectives
sections.content: Unlike Dravidian and Indo-Aryan languages which use a fixed consonant (such as gi- in Tamil or v- in Hindi) for echo formation, Tangkhul constructs echo compounds through semantic pairings of near-synonyms or coordinate clan items. The compound signifies not merely the literal items but the entire cultural domain or household equipment.

sections.title: 2. Tonal Acoustic Measurements & F0 Contours

title: Tangkhul Luira Phanit (Seed Sowing Festival) and Ancient Agricultural Invocations

journal: Journal of North East India Council for Social Science Research & TRI Manipur

subject: Ethnolinguistics, Cultural Anthropology & Ritual Chants
notes: Classic ethnolinguistic study by Prof. Khashim Ruivah documenting the ritual prayers, chants, and dance song texts of Luira Phanit.
abstract: Luira Phanit (the Seed Sowing Festival) is the supreme cultural and agricultural festival of the Tangkhul Naga people, celebrated annually in February across all traditional villages. This paper provides an ethnolinguistic documentation of the ceremonial liturgy performed during Luira. We record and translate the sacred Chithar (first seed-sowing invocation) chanted exclusively by the village chief (Awungshi), the liturgical formulas for domestic hearth renewal, and the poetic lyrics of the Hao Pheichak (traditional circle dance). The texts preserve archaic lexical roots unrecorded in modern dictionaries.

The festival extends across seven ceremonial days: Luishat (preparation), Phanit-khara (arrival), Pheichak (communal dance), and Ngashan (clan feasting).

title: Tangkhul Hao Ngashan: Customary Law, Clan Exogamy, and Social Governance
alternate_titles: Jurisprudence, Kinship Systems, and Conflict Resolution in Tangkhul Customary Law
journal: Tribal Jurisprudence & Cultural Bulletin of Manipur
publisher: Wung Cultural Research Forum / Directorate for Development of Tribals, Imphal
subject: Customary Law, Tribal Jurisprudence & Clan Governance
notes: Definitive codification and analysis of Tangkhul customary jurisprudence, clan exogamy, and village court administration.
abstract: Hao Ngashan embodies the unwritten constitutional and customary legal code governing Tangkhul society since time immemorial. This paper analyzes the structural pillars of Tangkhul customary jurisprudence: the patrilineal clan system (Shang), strict clan exogamy (Kashan), land tenure mechanisms, the judicial authority of the Village Council (Hangva), and traditional dispute settlement procedures. We examine the sacred oath-taking formula (Tuishot) and demonstrate how customary law operates harmoniously alongside modern constitutional protections in Manipur.

sections.title: 1. The Clan (Shang) and Exogamous Marriage (Kashan)
sections.content: Tangkhul social structure is organized into patrilineal clans (Shang) that trace their descent from common ancestors. The bedrock principle of social ethics is Kashan—strict clan exogamy. Intermarriage within the same Shang is considered an intolerable moral taboo (Kashansha) that historically incurred banishment from the village territory. All marriages must link distinct Shangs, creating enduring reciprocal obligations and alliances across the community.

sections.title: 2. The Village Court (Hangva) & Judicial Administration
sections.content: Civic, property, and criminal disputes are adjudicated by the Hangva (Village Council and Court of Elders), presided over by the hereditary Awungshi (chief). Each major clan is represented by a senior elder (Hangva-khana). The court prioritizes reconciliation (Tui-ngalung) and restitution rather than retributive punishment. Fines historically took the form of cattle, swine, woven blankets (Haora), or rice beer (Khor).

title: Tangkhul Kinship Terminology, Consanguinity, and Lineage Structure: An Ethnolinguistic Model
alternate_titles: Ethnolinguistic Analysis of Tangkhul Naga Kinship Terms
subject: Ethnolinguistics & Kinship Anthropology
notes: Comprehensive ethnolinguistic analysis classifying Tangkhul kinship terminology within the bifurcate merging Omaha type.
abstract: Kinship terminologies embody the social structural logic and reciprocal obligations of human societies. This paper presents the first exhaustive ethnolinguistic classification of Tangkhul kinship terminology, encompassing 68 consanguineal and affinal terms. We demonstrate that Tangkhul exhibits a bifurcate merging system of the Omaha subtype, reflecting strict patrilineal clan organization (Shang) and asymmetrical cross-cousin marriage rules.

sections.title: 1. Bifurcate Merging & Patrilineal Alignment
sections.content: In Tangkhul, the father's brother is addressed by the same root as father (Ava-kakhano for father's younger brother, Ava-kakhara for father's elder brother), whereas the mother's brother is distinguished as Mawa/Kuku. Similarly, parallel cousins are equated with biological siblings (Uningnao), whereas cross-cousins fall into distinct terminological classes linked to marriageability.

sections.title: 2. Sibling Terminology & Seniority Distinctions
sections.content: Seniority relative to the speaker is strictly encoded in sibling terms. Elder brother is achon/ayei, younger brother is atat/akhanao, elder sister is va-kakhara, and younger sister is va-kakhano. The collective compound uningnao encompasses all sibling kin within the Shang lineage.

sections.title: 3. Affinal Terminologies & Asymmetrical Alliances
sections.content: Affinal terms reflect mother's brother's daughter (MBD) preferential alliance. The wife's clan is honored as Mayāng-shang (life-giving in-laws), commanding ceremonial gifts of meat and woven shawls at all lifecycle rituals.

title: Grammaticalization of Motion Verbs into Directional Postpositions in Tangkhul
alternate_titles: Spatial Deixis and Path Markers in Tangkhul Verbal Syntax
subject: Syntax, Semantics & Grammaticalization
notes: Traces the diachronic evolution of lexical motion verbs (kava 'go', khura 'come', kashok 'exit') into directional aspect auxiliaries.
abstract: This paper investigates the grammaticalization pathways through which full lexical motion verbs in Tangkhul have developed into directional markers, telic aspectual affixes, and spatial postpositions. Drawing on connected texts spanning a century of documentation, we demonstrate that motion verbs specifying vertical axis (ascent/descent) and deictic orientation (centrifugal vs centripetal) systematically fuse with verbal stems to form complex path predicates.

title: Optimality Theoretic Account of Tone Sandhi in Tangkhul Nominal Compounding
alternate_titles: Constraint Interaction and Prosodic Phonology of Tangkhul Pitch
journal: Phonological Studies of the North East (NEILS Occasional Papers)
subject: Theoretical Phonology & Optimality Theory
notes: First Optimality Theory (OT) constraint-based analysis of tone sandhi and register raising in Tangkhul noun compounding.
abstract: When monosyllabic morphemes concatenate into compound nouns in Tangkhul Naga, systematic tonal alternations occur to avoid adjacent sharp pitch falls within the prosodic word. This paper formulates an Optimality Theoretic (OT) analysis of Tangkhul tone sandhi. We show that the interaction of markedness constraints (*NoExtremeDrop, OCP-Tone) ranked above faithfulness constraints (Ident-IO(Tone)) successfully accounts for right-edge register raising.

sections.title: 1. The Empirical Problem of Tangkhul Sandhi
sections.content: Standard Ukhrul Tangkhul possesses three tones: High (H, 55), Mid (M, 33), and Low (L, 21). When a High-toned base compounds with a Low-toned nominal root, the surface output is consistently High-Mid (H-M) rather than the expected H-L. For example, luí (H, field) + ram (L, land) surfaces as [luí-ram] with Mid pitch on the second syllable.

sections.title: 2. OT Constraint Hierarchy
sections.content: We propose the constraint ranking: *Drop-HL >> OCP(Tone) >> Ident-IO(Tone). The high-ranked markedness constraint *Drop-HL prohibits a two-register pitch plunge (55 to 21) within a single prosodic word. Candidate [55-33] incurs a single violation of low-ranked faithfulness Ident-IO(Tone), but decisively eliminates the faithful candidate [55-21].

sections.title: 3. Compound Truncation and Coda Effects
sections.content: Syllables with glottal stop codas inhibit sandhi raising, behaving as opaque phonological boundaries. This demonstrates that laryngeal features interact directly with tonal autosegmental licensing in Tangkhul phonology.

title: Syllable Weight and Metrical Structure in Ukhrul Tangkhul
alternate_titles: Prosodic Phonology, Moraic Structure, and Stress Assignment
journal: Journal of the Linguistic Society of North East India
publisher: Linguistic Society of North East India, Imphal
subject: Metrical Phonology & Prosody
notes: Moraic phonological analysis mapping light (CV) vs heavy (CVC, CVV) syllables to stress assignment and foot binarity.
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between syllable weight, moraic structure, and stress assignment in Standard Ukhrul Tangkhul. While Tangkhul has traditionally been described as a tone language without prominent stress, acoustic analysis reveals that primary metrical stress consistently falls upon the final heavy syllable (bimoraic μμ) of the phonological stem, relegating light prefixal syllables (monomoraic μ) to metrically weak prosodic positions.

sections.title: 1. Syllable Typology and Mora Count
sections.content: Tangkhul syllables conform to the maximal template (C)(C)V(C). Syllables ending in vowels (CV) are monomoraic (light, μ), while syllables closed by sonorant or stop codas (CVC) and syllables with diphthongs (CVV) are bimoraic (heavy, μμ). Only bimoraic syllables can carry the full three-way tonal contrast in citation form.

sections.title: 2. Metrical Foot Binarity & Iambic Grouping
sections.content: Disyllabic prefix-stem words form canonical iambic feet (L H), where the light prefix serves as the weak foot member and the heavy root serves as the rhythmic head. This explains why prefix vowels are phonetically reduced to schwa [ə].

sections.title: 3. Rhythmic Implications for Folk Verse
sections.content: Traditional Tangkhul oral poetry (Hao-laa) exploits this bimoraic foot structure. Chants are organized into four-mora hemistichs, establishing a steady musical pulse that coordinates choral dancing during festivals.

title: Ethnobotanical Wisdom and Traditional Herbal Medicine of the Tangkhul Nagas
alternate_titles: Indigenous Phytotherapy, Sacred Plants, and Forest Ecology of Ukhrul
journal: Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge (IJTK / CSIR-NIScPR)
subject: Ethnobotany, Traditional Medicine & Ecology
notes: Comprehensive documentation of 85 medicinal plants, indigenous taxonomic classifications, and healing formulas used by Tangkhul herbalists.
abstract: The biodiverse montane forests of Ukhrul and Kamjong districts harbor an extraordinary repository of botanical species. This paper documents the traditional ethnobotanical knowledge of the Tangkhul Nagas based on ethnopharmacological fieldwork with 14 practicing village herbal healers (Khangashun-Kaphānao). We catalogue 85 medicinal plant species across 42 families, detailing native Tangkhul nomenclature, plant parts used, preparation modes, and therapeutic applications for fevers, bone fractures, digestive ailments, and poison antidotes.

sections.title: 1. Native Botanical Taxonomy (Tangkhul Plant Classification)
sections.content: Tangkhul folk taxonomy organizes the plant kingdom into major morphological life-forms: Thingphun (large standing timber trees), Wonra/Tingra (climbing lianas and woody vines), Shinao/Khangaphei (herbaceous forest floor plants), and Thingthei (fruit-bearing flora). Medicinal efficacy is categorized according to taste qualities: kakhui (bitter/antipyretic), kashā (pungent/anti-inflammatory), and ngam-kasa (sweet/tonic).

sections.title: 2. Key Medicinal Species & Indigenous Preparations
sections.content: Foremost among Tangkhul therapeutic herbs is Zingra (Houttuynia cordata), used raw for digestive and antimicrobial cures. The bark of Thing-kakhui (Mahonia manipurensis) is boiled into an intense yellow tonic for jaundice and malaria. Fresh poultices of Won-khamathā (Clerodendrum colebrookianum) are applied to regulate hypertension and cardiac distress.

sections.title: 3. Conservation Ethics & Sacred Groves (Khamasung)
sections.content: Harvesting medicinal plants is governed by customary taboos (Khamasung). Healers never uproot entire plant colonies, harvesting only mature leaves or lateral roots while chanting prayers of apology to the forest spirit (Luiram Ameo). This ecological ethic preserved rare montane herbs for centuries.

title: Tangkhul Weaving and Textile Semiotics: Cultural Codes of Haora, Luirim, and Kashan
alternate_titles: Textile Anthropology, Color Symbolism, and Loom Technology in Ukhrul
publisher: Institute of Cultural Research & Handicrafts Development, Imphal
subject: Textile Anthropology, Weaving Semiotics & Material Culture
notes: Authoritative semiotic analysis of traditional Tangkhul loin-loom textiles, deciphering clan identity codes in Haora, Luirim, and Phingkham.
abstract: Traditional handloom textiles constitute one of the most sophisticated visual languages and identity markers in Naga civilization. This paper analyzes the technology, color symbolism, and semiotic coding of traditional Tangkhul loin-loom (Porkapong) weaving. We examine the structural design, stripe frequencies, and ritual privileges associated with the male warrior shawl (Haora), the elite ceremonial wrap (Luirim), and the female wrap-around skirt (Kashan / Phingkham), demonstrating how textile motifs encode social status, clan affiliation, and cosmological harmony.

sections.title: 1. Loom Technology: The Traditional Loin Loom (Porkapong)
sections.content: Tangkhul weaving is executed exclusively by women on the indigenous backstrap or loin loom (Porkapong / Khashan-thing). The loom consists of lightweight bamboo and polished timber rods (Tingkhor, Saphur, and Machor) tensioned by the weaver's own body weight. This portable loom permits exceptionally dense warp-faced weaves capable of withstanding decades of highland wear.

sections.title: 2. Color Semiotics and Structural Motifs: Haora & Luirim
sections.content: Color palettes are drawn from native natural dyes: Meithai-ra (wild madder) for deep crimson red, Kharong-thing (indigo leaves) for deep raven black, and unbleached cotton for virgin white. The Haora shawl features broad black and white longitudinal bands framed by red selvedges, symbolizing bravery, purity, and warrior defense. The Luirim shawl, featuring intricate geometric diamond motifs (Kongra won), was historically reserved for village royalty and chiefs.
